chapter_theme: Desire for another man's wife is the height of folly and a loss in every register at once. The chapter speaks to men, frames the woman as belonging to another, and calls restraint here the greatest manhood.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the faults of one who desires another's wife (141-146) and the virtues of one who doesn't (147-150). The verses also trace the act through its stages: desiring, standing at the door, entering, looking and touching.

141.reading: The folly of desiring a woman who is another's possession doesn't exist in those who have seen virtue and wealth in this world.
141.nuance: பிறன்பொருளாள், the verse's own word, treats the woman as property. Parimelazhagar explains why only two of the three aims are named: the science of pleasure has a term for this very act, so its experts can't be cited against it.

142.reading: Among all who stand outside virtue, none is a greater fool than those who stand outside another man's door.
142.nuance: The repeated கடை sets one threshold on another: outside virtue and outside the door. Parimelazhagar's reason is telling: other sinners at least get their pleasure, whereas this man is too afraid even for that. So the charge is stupidity, and even pleasure is lost.

143.reading: Those who take to evil in the home of people who trust them are surely no different from the dead.
143.nuance: The wrong here is defined by trust, as தெளிந்தார் shows: Parimelazhagar points out that the act is only possible because the husband trusts him. It's betrayal of a friend as much as sexual wrongdoing.

144.reading: However great they are, what does it come to, when one enters another's home without weighing it even a millet's worth?
144.nuance: A millet's worth of thought would be enough to stop it. Parimelazhagar names Indra as the example of greatness lost. He also reports a reading of தேரான் பிறன் as 'the unsuspecting husband'.

145.reading: One who crosses into a home thinking it easy gets blame that never dies.
145.nuance: The contrast is in timescale: 'easy' describes one moment and the blame lasts forever. Parimelazhagar makes it the family's blame, so the cost falls on others too.

146.reading: Enmity, sin, fear and blame: these four never leave one who crosses into a home.
146.nuance: The four cover different kinds of consequence: social, moral, psychological and reputational. 'Home' throughout this chapter stands for the wife, an equation that the Tamil title itself makes.

147.reading: The one called a householder in the way of virtue is he who doesn't desire the womanhood of the one who belongs to another's way.
147.nuance: It's a negative definition of the householder, after chapter 5's positive ones. Parimelazhagar makes it exclusive: he alone is such a householder.

148.reading: The great manhood that doesn't look at another's wife is, for the worthy, both virtue and complete conduct.
148.nuance: Parimelazhagar's explanation is a fine one: those who can subdue outer enemies can still find this inner enemy hard, so this is the greater manhood. He takes நோக்காத beyond looking, to not holding her in mind.

149.reading: Who deserve good on this world ringed by the awesome sea? Those who don't touch the shoulders of a woman belonging to another.
149.nuance: The question-and-answer form and the immense sea are grand for such a plain answer. தோள் is the vocabulary of love poetry. The commentators differ on நாமநீர், as Parimelazhagar has fearful water and Manakkudavar has water that grants wishes.

150.reading: Even if one doesn't practise virtue and does what is wrong, it's good not to desire the womanhood of one within another's bounds.
150.nuance: The verse sets a minimum for someone who has failed at everything else. Parimelazhagar says this quality alone stands out, and Manakkudavar says that it brings good even with no other virtue. It doesn't say the person is thereby virtuous.

links.note: Parimelazhagar uses Indra to illustrate both verses: 25 for the failure that shows the ascetic's power, and 144 for greatness lost through another's wife. This is one story serving two chapters in the commentary, though neither verse tells it.

Both call a living person effectively dead. In 80 it's the lack of love, and in 143, as both early commentators say, it's the loss of all three aims. A person can stop being alive in more than one way.

These are the two 'at least this' verses: however much else is left unguarded, guard the tongue; however wrong the rest, don't desire another's wife. They show what the book treats as the last line of moral defence.
Both define பேராண்மை, the same word. In 773 it is ferocity in battle whose edge is kindness, and here it is not looking at another's wife. The book redefines the warrior's virtue as self-mastery.

source_issues: The Tamil of verse 143 in kg/core has corrupted characters in விளிந்தா஡஢ன், which should read விளிந்தாரின் as Parimelazhagar's text shows.
Pope's text has typos in verse 145 ('triflel'), verse 146 ('ivades') and verse 150 ('dee ds').
